guide.title: What is programming?
guide.text: Programming means describing a task with precise instructions. The computer follows the language rules; it does not guess your intention.
guide.takeaway: Here the goal is to display 7. Change the number and the displayed result changes.

guide.title: From text to action
guide.text: A compiler analyses text and translates it into a form a runtime can execute. This game's small interpreter first builds a structure, then evaluates it.
guide.takeaway: Meaning comes from structure: add first, then display. This game does not run the full Tolang compilation pipeline.

guide.title: Mistakes are clues
guide.text: Syntax rules describe valid shapes. A missing parenthesis breaks that shape. A valid program can still do the wrong thing: displaying 8 is valid, but it does not meet a goal of 9.
guide.takeaway: First make the program valid, then check whether its actual result meets the task.

guide.title: Why count work?
guide.text: Different instructions can produce the same result with different amounts of work. Computing and storing data use resources. The step count here is only a model for learning.
guide.takeaway: Both display 5. The second needs an addition. These counts cannot predict TVM gas or transaction fees.

guide.title: Tolang and a blockchain
guide.text: Tolang is used to write programs for ALUX. On a blockchain, changing shared state also involves transaction rules and agreement between nodes. Language and execution environment both matter.
guide.takeaway: Displaying a number in this game sends no blockchain transaction. These first ideas also help you learn other programming languages.

guide.title: Choose and repeat
guide.text: A comparison produces true or false. if chooses a branch; for traverses a list or range, and while repeats while its condition is true. Tolang’s and and or evaluate both sides, so they do not protect a division by zero on the other side.
guide.takeaway: Predict both the displayed values and the number of outputs. A different iteration count can change a movement plan.

guide.title: Return a value or reply
guide.text: sync fn with return value produces a call-stack result. return ! value sends a function reply. Write the return explicitly: a function does not automatically return its last expression. A missing reply can leave its caller waiting.
guide.takeaway: Fewer arguments can create a partially applied function. Too many arguments do not create extra parameters.

guide.title: Coordinate messages
guide.text: let parcel; creates a communication name. ! sends and ? receives. A joint receive uses & to wait until all matching messages are available. | composes concurrent work; its appearance does not promise which output comes first.
guide.code:
let a; let b;
{ a ! 4 | b ! 6 | ?(x <- a & y <- b) { (x + y).log() } }
guide.takeaway: If one message is missing, the receive stays waiting. Use a joint receive when later work requires both values.

chase.title: Starport Chase
chase.intro: Be the police or the thief. Read the street, write a plan and watch every signal change the chase.
chase.policeGoal: Catch the thief before the exit
chase.thiefGoal: Reach the exit before you are caught
chase.rules: You move first, then your rival moves one space. Land on a roadblock and you stay put, but your rival still moves. You can jump over a roadblock. The thief escapes at space 18; the police catch them by reaching or passing their position.
chase.clue: Look at the numbered positions. Plan the landing spots, not just the total distance.
chase.signalRule: Each output must be an integer from 1 to 3: the number of spaces you move. Print 1–8 signals in order. A chase ends as soon as someone is caught or escapes; later signals are not used.
chase.keyboard: Write the code here, then run it. Typing speed does not change the chase.
chase.ready: The street is waiting for your plan.
chase.changed: Plan changed. Run it again to see what happens.
chase.retry: Trace each landing and try another plan. Retrying costs nothing.
chase.meaning: let gives a value a name; + adds values; .log() prints a value. This game reads each printed number as a move. The same code can control different things in another game.
chase.local: Both roles’ drafts and completed districts stay in this browser. Login does not sync them. These missions are untimed.
